newsitem.title: USA: US platinum coins not seen boosting demand much.
newsitem.headline: US platinum coins not seen boosting demand much.

text.p: The decision by the U.S. government to go ahead with plans to issue platinum coins next year is not seen boosting platinum demand significantly, analysts said.
In the appropriations bill which passed through Congress Monday, the U.S. Mint was given authority to issue a platinum coin and a second type of gold coins.
The platinum coins would compliment U.S. Mint's gold and silver American Eagle bullion coins, analysts said.

"These platinum coin sales could begin early in 1997 and will increase the amount of platinum used in coins, with Canada and Australia already issuing platinum coins also," CPM Group analyst Joseph Rosta said.

U.S. Mint has been consulting with platinum refiners over the minting of the coins, analysts said, and the Mint's stocks of platinum are believed to be low, suggesting some demand for platinum will emerge from the program.

Under language used in the fiscal 1997 funding law, the Mint could use U.S. government stocks of platinum as working inventory to produce the platinum coins, but the reserves would have to be replenished.
"But in terms of a total addition to platinum demand, your're not talking about much of a boost," said Daniel Weissman, MTB Bank's chief precious metals trader in New York.
MTB Bank is a major player in the bullion coin market.

"We're in a bear market right now, so any good news in terms of demand is being ignored," he said. "The platinum coins are not as popular as other bullion coins and we're probably talking only about 30,000 ounces of platinum."

NYMEX October platinum futures were up $0.90 at $385.50 an ounce at midday Tuesday. But in the bullion market, platinum was fixed at $381.50 this morning in London, its lowest level since Jan 28, 1994.
